# My Thinking for This Year

I'm 79 years old now, and my wife and I are the only ones left on our 4.1 mu of land. Our son works in Shijiazhuang and sends some money back, but not much. I've been farming this land for 70 years — I know every corner of it, which patch is a bit higher and dries faster, where the soil is heavier. At my age, I can't lift like I used to, so I have to think carefully about what I can actually do myself and what I need to ask my nephew to help with.

We're about to plant winter wheat. I always grow wheat on all 4.1 mu, then maize right after harvest in June. That's what everyone around here does, and it works. I save my own wheat seed — I've been using the same local variety for years. It doesn't yield as much as the newfangled ones, but the seed is free and I know how it behaves. For maize, I buy hybrid seed from the shop. You can't really save maize seed, it doesn't work the second year.

For fertilizer, last year I put about 40 jin of compound fertilizer per mu as base for wheat, and then topdressed with urea at green-up. I think that worked out to roughly 14-15 kg of nitrogen per mu. The yield was decent — around 400 kg per mu. This year fertilizer prices are about the same, maybe a little high. I can't afford to cut back because at my age, I can't make up for poor soil with extra labor. I'll do about the same: one bag of compound fertilizer (about 50 kg) for the 4 mu as base — that's about 12-13 kg per mu — and then if the wheat looks yellow after winter, I'll spread some urea at jointing. I don't do soil tests, I just look at the plants.

For irrigation, we have the tube well, but pumping costs electricity and that adds up. For wheat, I'll irrigate three times if I can afford it: once before winter to help establishment, once at jointing in spring, and once at grain filling if it doesn't rain. Last year I only did twice because the electricity bill was worrying me. I'll try for three this year — the old saying is "wheat likes water at jointing."

For maize, the schedule is always tight. After we harvest wheat in early June, we have maybe a week to get maize in the ground. I hire my nephew with his small tractor to do the tillage and planting — I can't do that by hand anymore, not at my age. It costs about 200 yuan for the custom work on 4 mu. For maize fertilizer, I usually put down compound fertilizer at planting, about 10-11 kg nitrogen per mu. I irrigate maize once or twice, usually once at the V6 stage and maybe again at tasseling if it's dry. Some years I don't irrigate maize at all if the summer rains are good — last year I irrigated once.

Pesticides — I don't use much. For wheat, sometimes I spray for weeds in spring if I see a lot of them. For maize, I usually put down a pre-emergence herbicide because my back can't handle hoeing weeds in July heat. I hire someone to spray, about 30 yuan per mu.

Labor is our biggest constraint. My wife and I can handle the day-to-day things — spreading fertilizer by hand, turning the water on and off, harvesting wheat with a sickle (though it's getting hard). For planting maize and anything heavy, I pay my nephew or hire help. I figure we put in about 15 family days for wheat and 12 for maize, plus 3-4 hired days for the maize planting and any spraying.

For yields, I expect about 380-420 kg per mu for wheat if the weather cooperates. For maize, maybe 400-450 kg per mu. I'm not greedy — at my age, a stable harvest is better than a gamble.

Money is tight. Total input costs will be around 1,600-1,700 yuan for both crops. I have to keep some cash for medicine and emergencies, so I won't push for the "best" inputs. Good enough is good enough.
